=== [Final] 59142 Lancium_Google_Eolic Comments.pdf ===
                                     PROJECT NO. 59142

 REVIEW OF ERCOT'S                             §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF
 INTERCONNECTION PROCESSES                     §                  TEXAS
 FOR LARGE LOADS                               §

                        GOOGLE, EOLIC, AND LANCIUM JOINT
                         COMMENTS ON ERCOT’S PGRR 145

       Google LLC, Eolic Development Partners LLC, and Lancium LLC (together, the “Joint

Commenters”) appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the Electric Reliability

Council of Texas’s (“ERCOT”) Planning Guide Revision Request (“PGRR”) 145 in Project No.

59142. Joint Commenters support ERCOT’s and stakeholders’ ongoing efforts to develop a

workable Batch Zero framework that brings greater transparency, consistency, and predictability

to the planning and interconnection process for large loads in ERCOT. Those efforts have

produced meaningful progress. However, targeted modifications to the proposed Batch Zero

framework are still necessary to ensure that it fully advances Texas’ continued economic growth

through efficient, coordinated, and coupled load and transmission planning.



1.​    Joint Commenters recommend that all large load projects justifying the need for an

RPG transmission project submitted prior to April 1, 2026, should be modeled as base load

in the Batch Zero study and approved contingent on the identified transmission upgrades

being constructed.

       Joint Commenters strongly recommend that all large load projects reflected in ERCOT

Regional Planning Group (“RPG”) filings submitted by Transmission Service Providers

(“TSPs”) prior to April 1, 2026, and relied upon to establish the need for transmission upgrades,

should be modeled as base load in the Batch Zero study and approved with Load Commissioning

Plans (“LCPs”) aligned with the construction and energization of those upgrades. As Oncor


                                                1
 noted in its April 10, 2026 comments in Project No. 59142,1 many of these loads were submitted

and studied well before the current Batch Zero construct was under consideration and have

already been analyzed extensively through the RPG process. As AEP noted in its March 20,

2026 comments in ERCOT’s Batch Zero Workshop Process, “These RPG studies identify the

system upgrades necessary to serve the load and meet all transmission planning criteria for both

steady-state and stability, aligning with what is done in the LLIS process. The scope of RPG

studies goes beyond LLIS by evaluating alternatives, costs, and future load serving capability.

Many of these RPG submittals were in development well before the announcement of the effective

date for PGRR 115. As these loads will be re-evaluated in the Batch study process, AEPSC

believes an ERCOT acceptance or endorsement of the RPG should not be required as a threshold

eligibility requirement.”2 AEP further commented at the March 24, 2026 Batch Zero Workshop

that, in many cases, these RPG studies exceed the quality and actionability of other load studies

that may qualify for Batch Zero under the current draft because they reflect a comprehensive

transmission solution for all loads identified in the relevant RPG. For that reason, loads that have

already supported the identification and justification of transmission upgrades in a TSP-filed

RPG study submitted on or before April 1, 2026, should not be excluded as baseload from Batch

Zero. Including those loads, on a contingent basis tied to the completion of the associated

transmission facilities, is the more reasonable, efficient, and administrable outcome and best

serves the public interest.

          In addition to the rigorous level of study already performed on these loads, Joint

Commenters recommend the proposed inclusion criteria for the following three reasons.




1
    https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/59142_19_1620365.PDF
2
    https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/03/20/145PGRR-26-AEP-Comments-032026.docx


                                                   2
    A.​ Leveraging existing RPG transmission planning work will produce a more

       successful Batch Zero outcome for reliability, speed, certainty, and the amount of

       load that can be served.

       Batch Zero should be used to convert existing planning work into actionable approvals,

not to recreate studies already developed and submitted by TSPs in the RPG process. To put it

simply, some loads already have identified transmission solutions, and some have not. Loads that

have identified transmission solutions are the strongest candidates for Batch Zero baseload

treatment because the core objective of the batch process—determining whether and how the

system can serve the load—has already been met. For those projects, the remaining task is not to

start over, but to place the load and the enabling transmission on a coordinated approval path and

assign a Load Commissioning Plan (“LCP”) tied to the completion of the necessary upgrades.

       This approach is also consistent with ERCOT’s own stated rationale for Batch Zero

inclusion. At the April 14, 2026, special Reliability and Operations Subcommittee (“ROS”)

meeting, ERCOT explained that the relevant principle for inclusion was whether there has been a

“demonstration that some level of assessment has been performed on the ability of the system to

serve that load.” That is precisely what an RPG assessment provides. ERCOT also

acknowledged that Batch Zero could function as an expedited ERCOT Independent Review

(“EIR”) for RPG projects already in flight. Where the system impacts have already been assessed

and the transmission solution has already been identified, Batch Zero should be used to move

those projects forward as baseload without further unnecessary delay. Said another way, Batch

Zero should serve as an expedited EIR.

       Using existing RPG work also directly addresses, or at least substantially mitigates,

ERCOT’s identified “year 6” challenge. ERCOT has expressed concern that it may not have the




                                                3
 time or resources to develop year 6 transmission plans from scratch within the Batch Zero

timeline. RPG-supported projects give ERCOT a practical way to meet that constraint by relying

on transmission plans that have already been developed and studied. Leveraging that existing

work will allow Batch Zero to move faster, approve more actionable load, and support greater

investment in Texas.



   B.​ Pairing transmission approvals with the loads that drove them ensures that costs of

       transmission are shared and mitigated by the new loads.

       When new transmission is planned to serve specific large load projects, those specific

loads should advance on a corresponding approval path so they can take service and share in the

costs of facilities built mostly for their benefit. Allowing transmission to proceed without a

comparable path for the underlying load to begin operating would leave other customers to bear

costs for upgrades planned around loads that have not been given a clear path to energization. It

should also be noted that in many cases, these loads have already executed interconnection

agreements and provided financial security for network upgrades, or otherwise accepted direct

cost responsibility through mechanisms such as contribution in aid of construction (CIAC).

       This risk is not hypothetical. The Commission's recent large load forecasting rules in 16

T.A.C. § 25.370, together with ERCOT's recent comments on the CNP Modification to the

Baytown Area Load Project RPG submission, indicate a real possibility that RPG projects

submitted prior to April 1, 2026, could continue to advance under the prior substantiated-load

framework even if the associated loads are not included in Batch Zero. Transmission approvals

could thus proceed for projects planned around specific large loads while those same loads

remain outside the operative approval framework. Applying the same April 1, 2026 cutoff




                                                 4
 reconciles this mismatch and ensures transmission approvals are paired with the loads that

justified them.

       For the reasons stated above, Joint Commenters reiterate that the better approach is to

keep these elements together: where a large load has driven an RPG transmission solution, both

the transmission and the load should move through Batch Zero on a coordinated, coupled

baseload basis.



   C.​ Converting RPG projects and their loads to actionable development plans in Batch

       Zero provides the necessary certainty needed to secure energy infrastructure

       investment.

       Large load projects reflected in RPG filings submitted prior to April 1, 2026, should be

included in Batch Zero as baseload because many of those projects have already progressed

beyond forecasted demand and are now driving real transmission, commercial, and infrastructure

decisions. Many have executed site agreements, committed capital, and begun engaging with

generation developers and transmission providers. These projects need a credible, time-bound

path to energization rather than additional study to ensure that already-committed private

investments are not stranded.

       Including these projects in Batch Zero baseload, with Load Commissioning Plans

(“LCPs”) tied to the completion of the actionable TSP identified transmission upgrades, provides

that needed certainty. It converts existing RPG load assumptions into credible development

milestones and gives developers, utilities, and counterparties a clearer basis for moving forward

with procurement, financing, and construction decisions. That certainty is especially important

because large loads must also develop their energy supply plans. A clear Batch Zero approval




                                                5
 pathway allows those loads to bilaterally secure the energy supply arrangements they will require

through existing market structures, including new generation.

         By making pre-April 1, 2026, RPG-supported loads eligible for non-contingent Batch

Zero baseload approval and aligning their LCPs with transmission completion, the Commission

transforms existing planning data into a transparent and credible demand forecast, providing a

clearer signal to the broader market regarding the timing and scale of expected load growth in

ERCOT.Because significant new load will not materialize without adequate generation supply,

including these projects as baseload in Batch Zero is essential to securing timely and coordinated

energy infrastructure investment across Texas. .



2.​      ERCOT or the certified retail utilities should backfill allocated capacity when a load

elects to not move forward.

​        Joint Commenters agree with Oncor in their April 10, 2026, comments that a mechanism

to backfill allocated capacity for the situation when a load has elected not to move forward

should be created. Such a mechanism would significantly improve the efficiency of the batch

study process through more timely allocation of capacity, reduce the risk of losing payments

from large loads to pay for transmission, and reduce the workload associated with the refinement

study.

                                         CONCLUSION

​        Joint Commenters appreciate the opportunity to comment on the ongoing batch zero

design efforts and look forward to engaging further at future ERCOT stakeholder meetings.



Respectfully submitted,




                                                   6
 Christopher Matos                    Evan Neel
Energy Market Development Lead       Sr. Director, Regulatory and Power Services
Google LLC                           Lancium LLC




Shannon Caraway
President & Co-Founder
Eolic Development Partners LLC
